title: Kennedy Center Board Votes to Shut Down Facility Immediately After Judge Blocks Trump Again From Adding His Name to Building
description: President Donald Trump said the board of the Kennedy Center voted Tuesday to shut down the building for “safety reasons,” coming shortly after a fed
body:
President Donald Trump said the board of the Kennedy Center voted Tuesday to shut down the building for “safety reasons,” coming shortly after a federal judge again ruled that the performing arts center was legally prohibited from adding Trump’s name.

	In a post on Truth Social, Trump said the board of the Kennedy Center agreed “almost unanimously, to close the Building for Safety reasons, and so that it can begin the process of Reconstruction.” The closing will take place immediately, he said.
	

	However, Trump said, the renovation project “cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board’s approved name. If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place.” 


	Attorneys from the Justice Department will ask for “an expedited appeal” in the matter. A federal judge previously barred the Kennedy Center from shutting down as Trump had wanted. “In the meantime, 17 Million Dollars, raised by President Trump, has been put into The Kennedy Center account to keep it afloat,” Trump wrote in the post.

	The Kennedy Center board’s decision to shut down came after a judge again ruled that the addition of Trump’s name to the Kennedy Center violated federal law.

	On Tuesday, Judge Christopher Cooper of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ruled on an emergency motion seeking to block the board of the Kennedy Center — which is comprised of Trump loyalists — from adding his name in other places on the building and its grounds.
	

	“Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” Cooper wrote in his decision. “The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted.”

	In May, Cooper, an Obama appointee, ordered the center to remove Trump’s name from the building and other materials. The performing arts center complied with his order, and since then a tarp has covered the front façade.

	Despite that, Cooper wrote in the ruling, “the drama at the Kennedy Center continues. Despite the Court’s order, on August 13, 2026, the Board passed a resolution ‘to recognize and honor President Trump’s current and future existential and unprecedented contributions to the survival of the Center’ in three different ways.”

	Per the board’s resolution, on the façade below its official name, “The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts,” there would be an additional line reading “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.” The board also voted to designate “the physical site and grounds upon which the center sits” as the “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”

	Cooper granted the motion filed by Rep. U.S. Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), who had originally sued the Kennedy Center and Trump over the renaming, to block the proposed additions.

	Beatty is “entitled to enforcement of the Court’s injunction, which reflects Congress’s decision to memorialize President Kennedy, and no one else, at the Center bearing his name,” Cooper wrote. A copy of the decision is available at this link.

	In his ruling earlier this spring, Cooper also granted Beatty’s request for a preliminary injunction to block Trump from taking any further steps to close the institution. Trump had previously proclaimed that the Kennedy Center would shut down for two years starting July 4, 2026, to undergo a “complete rebuilding.”

	Trump, in a post earlier Tuesday on Truth Social, said the Kennedy Center was in a dangerous state of disrepair when he returned to the White House in 2025. “The Board of the Kennedy Center has strongly voted to save it, and they know I’m the only one who can do so, because I have the ability to raise the money, and the ability to construct — that few others have. I also have the strength and power of the Presidency, which will be needed do what must be done, and give it a strong shot at Greatness again!” he wrote.
	

	Variety has reached out to reps from the Kennedy Center for additional information and comment.

schema.headline: Kennedy Center Board Votes to Shut Down Facility Immediately After Judge Blocks Trump Again From Adding His Name to Building

title: Ed Sheeran Opener Aaron Rowe Pulls Out of Tour After Macklemore Dropped: ‘I Cannot Allow Billionaires to Silence Rightful Voices’
description: Singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe has dropped out as an opener on the North American leg of Ed Sheeran‘s Loop tour after fellow supporting act Macklemore
body:
Singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe has dropped out as an opener on the North American leg of Ed Sheeran‘s Loop tour after fellow supporting act Macklemore was dismissed for voicing his support for Palestine.

	In a post on Instagram, the Irish musician also expressed his support for Palestine while explaining why he decided to leave the trek. “I have made the decision to withdraw as a support act for Ed Sheeran’s ‘The Loop’ North American Tour,” he wrote. “I don’t take the decision lightly. Ed has been a friend to me and has changed my life, I could never thank him enough for this.
	

	“But as Irish people,” he continued, “we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation. I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children. I would lose all respect for myself to carry on as normal. I need to be true to myself and my ancestors who resisted colonisation, and fought for a freedom that I enjoy today in Ireland.” He ended his note by declaring, “Free Palestine.”



	Rowe opened on the Australian leg of the Loop earlier this year and resumed as a supporting act in June for North American dates. Fellow opening act Lukas Graham remains on the bill for when the tour continues on September 19 in Philadelphia, while Finneas is slated to support South American shows in November.

	Rowe’s departure from the Loop tour comes after Macklemore was kicked off following forceful “free Palestine” comments made while opening for Sheeran at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sept. 4 and 5. Macklemore released a statement on Monday in which he accused billionaire New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft of rallying fellow stadium owners to ban the rapper from the tour due to his comments.
	

	Sheeran himself weighed in on Tuesday morning, explaining that he had nothing to do with the decision to eject Macklemore from the tour and that it had been at the discretion of the promoters and venues. He explained that he preferred to remain publicly neutral on political issues and that he is “not complicit” in doing so.

schema.headline: Ed Sheeran Opener Aaron Rowe Pulls Out of Tour After Macklemore Dropped: ‘I Cannot Allow Billionaires to Silence Rightful Voices’

title: Karina Longworth on ‘The Bisexuals,’ the Latest Season of Her ‘You Must Remember This’ Podcast:  ‘Even Progressive People’ Say ‘Bisexuality is a Myth’
description:

	After 18 seasons of her “You Must Remember This” podcast, former film critic L
body:
Karina Longworth isn’t that interested in modern Hollywood anymore.

	After 18 seasons of her “You Must Remember This” podcast, former film critic Longworth says she doesn’t pay much attention to the industry. She’s too busy digging up stories from old Hollywood, from gossip and feuds to controversies and murders.

	The latest season, “The Bisexuals,” launches Tuesday. Across eight episodes, Longworth explores the history of entertainment industry bisexuals through the lives of Broadway torch singer Libby Holman and movie star Montgomery Clift.
	

	Longworth is taking films from “You Must Remember This” on tour this fall with stops in Houston, New York, Boston, Chicago and more. Although Longworth prefers these classics over modern movies, her husband, filmmaker Rian Johnson, is behind a number of more recent Hollywood titles, including the “Knives Out” series and “Star Wars: The Last Jedi.”


	Before the launch of “The Bisexuals,” Longworth spoke with Variety about the season and her upcoming fall tour.
	
		What is it that keeps you digging into old Hollywood and keeps you engaged with so many new seasons of the podcast?	

	I just keep finding stories that I want to tell. I feel like the older I get, the less I’m interested in contemporary Hollywood. I used to be somebody that would go to the movies two or three times a week, and I don’t do that anymore. I probably see 10 or 12 new movies a year, and I have replaced that by watching so much stuff from classical Hollywood. Every time that I read a new book, I get new ideas, and then I want to watch all the movies discussed in the book, and then that leads me down these rabbit holes. I’ll keep doing the podcast until I either run out of ideas or nobody wants to listen to it anymore.
	
	
		Why did you start with Libby Holman, who’s not literally in Hollywood but is connected to so many people in show business?	

	The podcast season is more of a dual biography of Libby and Montgomery Clift, but it starts with Libby’s story because I like to tell stories chronologically. For a long time, I resisted doing a podcast even involving Libby — even though I was fascinated with her story — because of the fact she’s not a Hollywood creature at all. She never starred in a movie; she never lived in Los Angeles for any long length of time. She was a New York torch singer, Broadway star, and then, after a massive scandal in the 1930s, she continued to try to have a career as a singer to mixed results. It was a hurdle I had to get over in terms of thinking of my podcast as being Hollywood stories and trying to figure out if there was enough Hollywood content here. What I ended up figuring out was, first of all, it can be a split biography between her and Montgomery Clift, and I loved an excuse to watch all the movies of his that I hadn’t seen and revisit the ones I had. Then there’s also other people in their lives that were involved in films like Tallulah Bankhead and Clifton Webb, and then there’s these movies that are about Libby. It was really exciting to be able to discover some of them, but then also to be able to reframe the way I looked at something like “Written on the Wind” as being a story about Libby.
	
		You talk about all of the productions that are inspired by Libby and how she reacted to that. You look at those as something that was inspired by her life, but a lot of these change or add new characters or change the gender of some characters, which is especially interesting given that this season is talking about her as a bisexual.	

	I think the movie that you’re referencing is “Reckless,” which is directed by Victor Fleming, starring Jean Harlow as the Libby character and Franchot Tone as the version of her first husband, Smith Reynolds, and then it stars William Powell as the third leg of this love triangle as her benefactor, and that role was played in real life by a woman named Louisa Carpenter. It was definitely not something that a Hollywood movie of the 1930s was going to deal with. The idea that a woman could have both a husband and a girlfriend, or that a woman could have a girlfriend at all. Sometimes these things were implied. Somebody like Marlene Dietrich kisses a woman on screen in “Morocco.” But for the most part, this was not something that Hollywood was going to go that deep into, especially after the production code was enforced in 1934, which would put pretty strict rules in the way sexuality was depicted on screen. “Reckless” is also the only film that I could find that Libby commented on. She was really upset at this major motion picture with a big star that was about her story, even though some of the details were changed and the names were changed. Maybe the fact that the details were changed is one of the reasons why she was upset about it, and she thought about suing but decided not to. I have empathy for Libby’s experience there, but I also think “Reckless” is a really good movie, and I hope people check it out.
	
	
		It’s also a big stereotype about bisexual people in general that they are more sexually promiscuous because they are interested in both genders. Did that play into how you researched that or how you talked about that throughout the season?	

	I was interested in making a podcast season called “The Bisexuals” in part because I think bisexuality is misunderstood and often misrepresented. Even progressive people, even people who are very queer-friendly or even queer themselves will say that bisexuality is a myth. People say that, or they at least joke about it. Especially when it comes to somebody like Montgomery Clift, his persona went from projecting being a straight man when he was alive and working in Hollywood. Later, people seem to understand that he had relationships with men and branded him as gay. But then finding out the depth of his relationships and the fact that they were sexual, that made me understand that his sexuality was more complicated than even what is considered the progressive read on his sexuality. That was just really interesting to me. I didn’t want to talk about bisexuality in terms of it being a myth or the tropes that people attach to it.
	
		What stood out to you as you were looking at the perception of bisexuality?	

	I was interested in this idea that progress in terms of sexuality, but also in terms of other social issues, is not linear. It’s a pendulum that swings back and forth. It was interesting to me to read about Libby’s sexual and social life in the 1920s. She was perceived as somebody who was both racially and sexually fluid, and a lot of her social life took place in Harlem, where white people would go to engage in a kind of sex tourism. For Libby, it was not that she went up there to have sex with Black people. It was that, in the clubs up there, there was a safe space for her and her other queer female friends to express themselves more freely in public. They still were doing that in speakeasies down near Broadway, but they were able to have a little bit more freedom in this other community. In general, she had much more freedom being somebody who was involved with both men and women than Montgomery Clift did years later when he was a Hollywood star who was somebody who did have relationships with women like Libby but was sleeping with men. The part of his life where he was sleeping with men, he had to keep totally secret from the public. I was just really interested in how there was a possibility to be a famous person in 1920s New York and have people understand that there was a queerness to you, and that possibility was not available if you were a male movie star in the 1950s.
	
	
		The time periods were different, Montgomery was a man while Libby was a woman and not part of Hollywood. Were those intersections and things that were converging in both of their identities something that you wanted to peel back the layers on?	

	In the theater world in New York City, I think there was always an understanding and acceptance that people have a variety of sexual identities. It probably was not as open in the 1920s as it is now, but it was certainly more open than Hollywood was in the 1950s, and partially because of the production code, which was enforced in 1934. That came about, in part, as a response to scandals that happened off-screen in the 1920s. It was a way of cleaning up Hollywood’s image after things like the Fatty Arbuckle scandal. There was this idea that, in both on screen and off screen, Hollywood needed to keep things that were considered unacceptable to a middle American and generally Catholic point of view secret or hidden, or not have it represented in movies. Movies have a narrative on screen, and then there’s also the narrative off-screen about the stars and the people who make movies, and so there was this idea that whether it’s queerness, whether it’s interracial coupling, whatever it is, the stuff that wasn’t allowed in movies was also not allowed off screen. And if it was happening, then it had to happen under a cover. This is why somebody like Rock Hudson was encouraged to marry his female secretary. This is why Montgomery Clift was set up on dates with people like Elizabeth Taylor. In that case, it turned out well. They became extremely close friends. They really loved each other, even if their love was not sexual. But nobody was trying to set Libby Holman up with a man in order to sanitize her image, and in the late 1920s in New York City, nobody wanted a sanitized image.
	
		One of my favorite lines was that there was a “cultural capital in racial ambiguity” and that Libby was afforded the luxury of letting people read into whatever she was playing up. What do you think that was like for her?	

	Libby was a Jewish girl from Cincinnati who moved to New York City, and she had a slightly olive complexion, but really, it was because of the way she sang, in a deep, throaty voice, singing what we would now call blues songs. People started gossiping that she must be Black trying to pass as white, and she wasn’t. But she let people think that, and she even talked later about how she felt flattered by that misinterpretation of her identity, and that she was excited by it. She thought it made her cooler, and it did help her, I think, in her career at this time. She became very famous in this show called “The Little Show,” in which her big number and what would become her signature song was called “Moanin’ Low.” This is a classical torch song in that it’s a dirge about a woman loving that a man treats her badly, and they dramatize this on stage with her and Clifton Webb, who I talk about later in the podcast. He was a gay man who became a movie star as a character actor, but as a movie star, not being open about his sexuality, but at times playing characters that felt like they had a little bit of a queerness to them. He and Libby are on stage, and he’s playing her pimp, and she’s playing a sex worker, and they’re both wearing black makeup. It’s not shoe black the way that we’ve seen blackface in movies. It’s designed to be more natural, for lack of a better word. It’s designed to look like a Black person, and this was considered normal for a drama of sexual violence on stage at that time. Libby was already considered to be racially ambiguous. She was not perceived as somebody who was white. It was not considered a huge departure for her to do this kind of number, and in fact, it really created her stardom. I found that to be very fascinating, particularly since, as far as I can tell from the many, many materials I read about this, there was no conversation about whether or not this was racist or offensive to Black people, and there was a conversation in the culture about blackface for sure by this time. But in this case, she was welcomed to sing at the Apollo Theater. She was to some extent embraced by a certain Black establishment.
	
	
		How do you reconcile things like that with a modern perspective on things that were happening?	

	That’s a lot of the reasons why I wanted to tell this story. When I first read about Libby Holman in Jon Bradshaw’s book about her, “Dreams that Money Can Buy,” I did this very close reading of that book where I’m constantly underlining passages and writing in the margins, like questions and commentary. It felt like there was so much about the racial stuff and the sexual stuff that was not interrogated or was framed in a way that was insulting and belittling. That was the stuff that I was excited to dig into, this thornier stuff. I don’t think of Libby as being a role model or somebody where we can embrace every aspect of her without criticism. What was exciting to me was that she was an anti-heroine and somebody who made choices that today we would not accept at all. But she was also somebody who experienced tragedy, and I can criticize her and also have empathy for her.
	
		There’s a conversation about her potentially making racist remarks. You talk about how there are some reports that say that she said these things, but that also could have just been the person who was writing about it. How do you sort through those kinds of things where there might be conflicting reports?	

	I’ve come across this in many of the seasons I’ve done. I am a big believer of the fact that there is not one singular truth in most cases about anything, and the best I can do is be a transparent reader, and just talk about different accounts of things, and then make a conclusion that I’m being transparent about is my personal conclusion, as what is the most likely thing to be true. I just try to be really clear that I don’t know exactly what happened or which account to believe. It’s about making a collage of all these different accounts and then telling you what my interpretation is.
	
		You make comparisons to modern culture, such as white rappers or TikTok trends. How do you approach that?	

	It has been a way for me to understand it. We sometimes have this sense of history as being a musty old painting on the wall. But there’s always been young people. There’s always been a kind of counterculture. Some of the things that we’re experiencing right now in terms of new technology, for instance, and the way it’s upending culture, this was happening in the early 20th century in terms of airplanes. That just became the kind of thing that a young man with a lot of money would want to invest in, the way a young man today would want to invest in crypto. When I see parallels that help me understand history better, I want to share them.
	
	
		What can we expect from your tour this fall?	

	I’m super excited. We’ve announced most of the dates, but there’s gonna be some that are to be announced because of when the venues can put tickets on sale. I’m basically going to be on the road from October 3 until November 17, doing events at different repertory cinemas and historic theaters, showing movies from the podcast season. We’re showing everything from pre-code Tallulah Bankhead movies to some of these movies about Libby Holman to a wide variety of Montgomery Clift films. I was just excited to share the movies with people. I spent the past year studying film preservation at the George Eastman Museum, and while I was there, I gravitated towards exhibition, but also came to understand some of the reasons why certain films do not get distribution in terms of restorations of old films or films that have fallen out of availability because of rights issues. What I am really hoping to do with this tour, besides connect with the fans of the podcast and show them these movies, is to get a sense of how these different programmers in these different places approach showing classical Hollywood movies to their audiences, what their audiences want to see, and is there a way to open up space for some of these restorations that rarely get seen outside of archival situations?
	
		You’ve talked before about these old films and how difficult it can be to get access to them and see them anymore.	

	There’s several films that I talk about in this season where there is no commercial availability for them. The only way you can watch them, the way I watch them to talk about them, is by watching basically a bootleg that you find on a free video streaming site. I don’t think that for a movie released by a major studio in the 20th century, that we should have to be criminals to watch them. Unfortunately, because I went to film preservation school and specifically studied this issue, I now have a more complex understanding of many of the reasons why a film like “Faithless,” for instance, is very difficult to watch. I’m still trying to figure out what I can do to help change the situation.

schema.headline: Karina Longworth on ‘The Bisexuals,’ the Latest Season of Her ‘You Must Remember This’ Podcast:  ‘Even Progressive People’ Say ‘Bisexuality is a Myth’

title: Thailand Film and Tourist Officials on the Rise of Thai Cinema, Global Productions and the Impact of ‘The White Lotus’
description:
Following a spike in popularity for Thailand’s film and TV industry, the country’s filmmakers and tourism officials want to make sure it lasts.

	Ni
body:
Following a spike in popularity for Thailand’s film and TV industry, the country’s filmmakers and tourism officials want to make sure it lasts.

	Nithee Seeprae, Cod Satrusayang, Raymond Phathanavirangoon and Banjong Pisanthanakun joined Variety at the Toronto International Film Festival to discuss Thailand’s growing presence in the global film industry, both in the original work of Thai filmmakers and the influx of international productions shooting across the country.
	

	Pisanthanakun, whose latest film “Inherit” debuted at TIFF, is one of the filmmakers helping to introduce Thai cinema to audiences around the globe. “It’s one of the best film festivals in the world, and I’m so excited that my film got the chance to premiere [at TIFF],” Pisanthanakun said during the Variety Global Conversation. “It’s a big opportunity for Thai horror.”

	Pisanthanakun is considered one of the defining voices of contemporary Thai cinema, with his film “Pee Mak” as the country’s highest-grossing title of all time. Pisanthanakun’s movies, plus films like “How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies,” have further established the country’s presence in the international film industry. The latter became the first Thai film shortlisted at the Oscars for Best International Film.

	Phathanavirangoon, the producer and founder of the SEAFIC Script Lab, says he’s noticed a new energy among Thai filmmakers, pointing to the rise of international productions coming to Thailand, such as “The Creator” and “Jurassic World: Rebirth,” as well as the country’s homegrown films.
	

	“Both sides go hand-in-hand to show people what Thailand actually has to offer, especially in terms of cinema,” Phathanavirangoon said.

	The panelists also discussed the impact of “The White Lotus,” which filmed its third season in Thailand. Satrusayang, the head of studio at TSixtySix, worked on the hit HBO series and says creator Mike White was deeply immersed in Thai culture and intended for it to serve as a love letter to the country. The season featured Thai actors and traditional dances, food and locations, all of which helped introduce viewers to different aspects of the country’s culture.

	After the island Koh Samui appeared in “The White Lotus,” online interest in the location spiked 88%, and the island’s hotel reservations increased by 44%. This increased visibility has also contributed to the rise of “set-jetting,” with audiences seeking out destinations they’ve seen on screen. The Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT) launched a new campaign, “Amazing Locations: From Scene to Scenic,” to capitalize on that interest and connect the country’s growing prominence as a filming destination with tourism.

	“We try to promote both sides,” Seeprae, the deputy governor of TAT explained. “I hope when audiences see a Thai movie or a movie shooting in Thailand, they will follow the movie to Thailand. And of course, also, the ‘Scene to Scenic’ [campaign] tries to encourage all the producers to shoot in Thailand too.”

	International productions continue to travel to Thailand for filming, with more than 383 productions coming to Thailand this year alone, says Seeprae, the deputy governor of TAT. Revenue income has increased by about 5% to 10%, nearing about 6 million Baht last year. The country has also seen a 5% to 10% increase in productions shooting in Thailand over the past year.

	Revenue has continued to grow, and the influx of projects has created additional employment opportunities for Thai crews. The booming business and government support are key to the industry’s success, but Phathanavirangoon notes that Thai crews can movie magic no matter how much can afford to spend.

	“At every single price point, there’s something there for you to shoot and there’s something there for you,” he said. “There’s a team there that’s ready to support you.”
	

	Thailand has notably been used to portray locations across Asia and has served as a backdrop for projects including “The Creator,” “Jurassic World” and “Star Wars.” With the growing success of Thai films and the country’s increased visibility on screen, filmmakers hope international audiences will continue engaging with Thai stories and culture rather than simply seeing Thailand as a stand-in for other locations.

	“The next step in the evolution of that is to make sure that the Thai side of the deal — the creators and the artists in Thailand — carry that forward by making Thai culture and Thai content appealing to an international audience so that the momentum doesn’t stop,” Satrusayang said.

	Satrusayang’s company works on international productions filming in Thailand. With the growth of the country’s local film industry, he recently launched a separate company focused on local-language content and empowering young Thai filmmakers. As Pisanthanakun sees it, “continuity” is the key to Thai cinema’s evolution.

	“Right now, it’s more and more genres that can travel, but in one year, only a few films can do that,” said Pisanthanakun, who also produces projects from up-and-coming talents. “I need more than that so people can see Thai films and Thai locations more than this.”

	Phathanavirangoon concurred: “If we do our job right, the future will be very bright because there are a lot of talents in Thailand, and we want to promote them and help them to show the country in the future.”

schema.headline: Thailand Film and Tourist Officials on the Rise of Thai Cinema, Global Productions and the Impact of ‘The White Lotus’

title: Netflix’s ‘The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey’ Sets Release Date, First Look at Melissa McCarthy and Clive Owen
description: The Netflix limited series “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey” will premiere on Dec. 10, with the streaming platform also releasing a first look photo o
body:
The Netflix limited series “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey” will premiere on Dec. 10, with the streaming platform also releasing a first look photo of Melissa McCarthy and Clive Owen as Patsy and John Bennett Ramsey.

	The series explores the unsolved murder of JonBenét, who died Christmas night in 1996. Her body was found in the basement of her family’s house just hours after she was reported missing, sparking public outrage and speculation.
	

	Emily Mitchell stars as the titular role alongside Garrett Hedlund, Alison Pill, Shea Whigham, Owen Teague, Clifton Collins Jr., Angus Caldwell, Jaime Ray Newman, Rory Cochrane and Chris Bauer. The cast also includes Will Patton, Jeremy Bobb, John Billingsley, Josh Stamberg, Margo Martindale and Tzi Ma.


	Richard LaGravenese serves as showrunner, writer and executive producer, with Anne Sewitsky directing and executive producing. The series was co-written by Harrison Query and Tommy Wallach, who also executive produce alongside McCarthy and Sewitsky. David C. Glasser, Ron Burkle, Bob Yari and David Hutkin executive produce for for 101 Studios.

	“The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey” was first reported to be in the works in March 2024 and completed production in January 2025. It was formally greenlit at Paramount+ that same year before moving to Netflix in July. 

	Netflix previously released “Cold Case: Who Killed JonBenét Ramsey” in 2024, timed near the 28th anniversary of Ramsey’s murder. It ultimately became the most-watched series on the streaming platform during the week of Nov. 25, totaling 13.4 million views in those seven days.
	

	See the first look photo of McCarthy and Owen below.

title: Quentin Tarantino to Publish ‘Cliff Booth’ Novel Before Brad Pitt and David Fincher’s Movie Streams on Netflix
description: Quentin Tarantino is writing a novel version of his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” spinoff “Cliff Booth.” It will debut later this year, timed to t
body:
Quentin Tarantino is writing a novel version of his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” spinoff “Cliff Booth.” It will debut later this year, timed to the release of the forthcoming film starring Brad Pitt, who reprises his Oscar-winning role as a longtime stuntman.

	Tarantino’s book is titled “The Adventures of Cliff Booth,” which differs slightly from the sequel movie’s moniker, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” David Fincher is directing the follow-up film for Netflix. Tarantino, who wrote the screenplay, also published a novelization of his 2019 feature “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” 
	

	Tarantino’s latest novel will be published on Dec. 8 by HarperCollins. That’s after “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” lands in Imax theaters on Nov. 25 and ahead of the movie’s Netflix bow on Dec. 23.


	“Cliff Booth,” both the novel and movie, take place in Hollywood, 1977 — eight years after the original story. In “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” Leonardo DiCaprio and Pitt portray an aging actor and his longtime stunt double who are struggling to find their place in show biz. Paying tribute to the golden age of Hollywood, “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” was set in the late 1960s against the backdrop of the Manson family murders, with Margot Robbie playing Sharon Tate, the up-and-coming actress married to director Roman Polanski.

	Although plot details for the sequel have been kept under wraps, the novel’s logline teases that “the Swinging Sixties are long gone — but Clifford Booth keeps on keeping on…War hero, stuntman, bartender, cinema projectionist…with the occasional “clandestine services” for his friends…” 
	

	Sony released “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” which was a critical and commercial hit. The movie earned more than $400 million at worldwide box office against a $90 million budget, in addition to 10 Oscar nominations and two wins. Netflix is producing the sequel, which carries a $200 million production budget.

	Tarantino decided against directing “Cliff Booth” because he’s long expressed a desire to retire after making 10 movies. He’s made nine already — “Pulp Fiction,” “Inglourious Basterds” and “Reservoir Dogs” among them — and he didn’t want a sequel to be his last.

	“I love this script, but I’m still walking down the same ground I’ve already walked,” Tarantino said last year on the “The Church of Tarantino” podcast. “It just kind of unenthused me. This last movie, I’ve got to not know what I’m doing again. I’ve got to be in uncharted territory.”

title: Creator-Media Entrepreneur Hopes to Help Influencers Expand Appearances in Ads
description: Why dispatch replications of Amish farmers, wise elderly doctors or financial gurus to various TikToks and other short-form videos when real people
body:
Why dispatch replications of Amish farmers, wise elderly doctors or financial gurus to various TikToks and other short-form videos when real people can do the exact same thing?

	A technology company that builds products for media users has introduced a new platform that gives advertisers and creators the ability to license individuals’ likenesses for use in an array of promotional videos.


	Avail, the company behind the new offering, sees a chance to cut down on A.I.-created fakes that purport to be real people. “I am seeing a deluge of fully synthetic creators on my feed, and, you know, to me personally, it’s a bit dystopic,” says Chris Giliberti, CEO and co-founder of Avail, during a recent interview. “You see these people that aren’t real, adverting products, and it used to be the case that this was a form of advertising all about authenticity. That was why you did it, you know? And now, it’s like it could not be more opposite.”
	

	The new tool, called creatorAPI, lets individual creators establish guidelines governing how brands may use their likeness, voice and performance, including which products, subjects, claims and creative treatments are permitted or off-limits. Advertisers can then generate different videos within those agreed-upon parameters. Marketers can buy and test different kinds of content while creators can take part in more campaigns without sacrificing additional time.


	Advertisers deploying short-form video are “often thinking in terms of how many different types of creative” can they deploy, says Giliberti. “You need all these different at- bats to find an asset that really works, that really pops.” He adds: “What we’re doing is we are giving brands the ability to multiply the number of at bats with a single creator.”
	

	With projections calling for the so-called “creator economy” to grow robustly in years to come, the Avail technology appears to offer a solution for a potential impediment. Consumers are growing more attached to individual hosts, creators and speakers who aren’t tied completely to mainstream media. And yet, these entrepreneurs can undermine their authenticity by placing themselves under the aegis of a marketer that doesn’t deploy their work in a way that is embraced by followers.

	A popular estimate from Goldman Sachs in 2023 called for the creator economy to grow to $480 billion by 2027 from $250 billion at the time.

	creatorAPI has been tested in closed beta with a small group of direct-to-consumer brands and creators, and is launching with Night Media, a digital talent management concern, and Emily Higgins, who has developed a following for creating popular videos about AI. The new technology “empowers me to extend the reach of a single campaign and gives brand partners testing flexibility. The appeal is the chance to enhance the performance of my content so both the brand and I win,” Higgins says in a statement.

	Avail’s technology puts a new spin on an old practice in the advertising industry. Marketers for years have tried to test tweaks in copy and in the kind of offer they make in a commercial, working to determine which version of an ad would carry the largest appeal to most people. This new service helps boost that process, says Giliberti.

	As a senior executive at Gimlet Media, a company known for its podcasts Giliberti often encountered marketers trying to produce the right commercial. “I just remember feeling like this is so full of friction, the way that this works,” he says. How are we ever going to get this transaction to be as smooth as programmatic advertising?” Indeed, over time, Avail expects to develop a system under which creators can increasingly negotiate, license, generate and execute campaigns through software, creating something closer to a programmatic marketplace for human creator advertising.

title: Netflix Sets ‘New Stanford Prison Experiment’ Unscripted Series for October Release (EXCLUSIVE)
description:

body:
Netflix has commissioned an unscripted series based on the notorious Stanford Prison Experiment, Variety has learned exclusively. 

	The series, titled “The New Stanford Prison Experiment,” will debut on Oct. 21. The first season will consist of six 45-minute episodes. A first-look photo from the series can be seen above. The official synopsis of the series states: 

	“Thirty willing participants enter a real prison and are randomly assigned as guards or prisoners. Thrust into a system of power, hierarchy, and control, they’ll discover whether ordinary people inevitably conform to the roles they’re given—or whether empathy, morality, and individuality can withstand the forces pushing them in the opposite direction. As the pressure builds and the balance of power begins to shift, the central question feels more urgent than ever: Does power corrupt?” 
	

	“The New Stanford Prison Experiment” is produced by Alfred Street Industries, with Jane Lipsitz, Dan Cutforth, Nan Strait, Dan Volpe, Jeff Grogan, and Mike Odair executive producing. 


	“The Stanford Prison Experiment has always fascinated me,” Lipsitz said. “Despite its serious ethical flaws, it asked a fundamental question that feels even more relevant today: how does power affect ethical choices? Getting the opportunity to reimagine this social experiment was one of the most intense, exhilarating — and definitely nail-biting — experiences we’ve ever had. Netflix has always been an incredible supporter of ambitious projects that take risks, push boundaries and tell challenging stories, so we were incredibly grateful to have them as our partners on this one.” 
	

	The Stanford Prison Experiment was conducted on the Stanford campus in 1971, led by psychology professor Philip Zimbardo. What was originally designed to be a two-week experiment was ended after less than a week when those assigned to be guards began abusing those assigned as prisoners, among other ethical concerns. This and other experiments around the same time period led to the adoption of stricter rules to prevent harm to human participants.  

	There have been multiple books, documentaries, docuseries, and scripted adaptations of the original experiment. Among those is the feature film “The Stanford Prison Experiment,” which was released in 2015 and starred Billy Crudup as Zimbardo.

title: Israel’s Oscar Entry ‘Tell Me Everything’ Finds International Distribution as Paradise City Sales Unveils Trailer (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Moshe Rosenthal’s “Tell Me Everything” continues to build momentum after winning 10 Ophir Awards, including best picture, best director and best scr
body:
Moshe Rosenthal’s “Tell Me Everything” continues to build momentum after winning 10 Ophir Awards, including best picture, best director and best screenplay, from a record-breaking 16 nominations.

	Israel’s submission for the international feature Oscar, the father-son drama has secured a string of international sales, including France (Maverick), as well as Australia and New Zealand (Moving Story) and Indonesia (PT Falcon). HBO CEE has also picked up digital rights across Central and Eastern Europe.
	

	The film premiered in Sundance’s World Cinema Dramatic Competition and has since screened at nearly 30 international festivals.


	Set against the pop culture boom of the late 1980s and the growing HIV epidemic, “Tell Me Everything” follows 12-year-old Boaz, who discovers a devastating secret about the father he idolizes. The revelation threatens to tear his family apart and leaves a wound that follows him into adulthood as he tries to rebuild the bond with his father.

	The film stars newcomer Yair Mazor and Ido Tako (The Vanishing Soldier”). Assi Cohen, one of Israel’s biggest comedy stars, takes on a rare dramatic role as Boaz’s father, while Keren Tzur (“Karaoke”) plays his mother. Mor Dimri and Neta Orbach also star.



	“Tell Me Everything” marks Rosenthal’s second feature following “Karaoke,” which premiered at the 2022 Tribeca Film Festival and went on to earn 14 Ophir nominations, including best film and best director. The film has since screened at more than 90 festivals, won a dozen awards and is being developed for remakes in several territories, including North America and Germany.
	

	“Tell Me Everything” is produced by Alona Refua, Maya Fischer, Roi Kurland and Gal Greenspan at Green Productions (“A Letter to David”); Ben Giladi at Liminal Content (“Karaoke”); and Moshe Edery and Leon Edery at United King Films (“Footnote”). 

	Émilie Georges and Naima Abed of Paradise City, whose credits include “Call Me by Your Name,” “Drift” and “Atropia,” are co-producers. Executive producers are Jonathan Margolis, Isaac Zablocki, Fred Toczek, Sharon Chazin Lieblein and Limor Gott Ronen.

            Porn star Christian Styles' death was caused by heavy drinking and kratom use ... which is called "gas station heroin" ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to Michigan’s Wayne County Medical Examiner … Christian died due to alcohol and mitragynine toxicity. Mitragynine is the active ingredient in Kratom, which is a product sold without a prescription for pain relief and energy.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The report says Christian had a 0.168 BAC, mitragynine, and several of its breakdown products in his blood. The porn star was found dead inside a bedroom in his home when his parents came to check on him.
      

            The report says Christian had been on a bender with various substances and had a history of abusing heroin and meth, and his parents had been checking on him hourly, with his last known alive time at 3 pm.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            His parents told investigators Christian had a history of ODs and other run-ins with law enforcement. No drugs were found at the scene, but an accidental OD was suspected.
      
    
            Christian was 29. He became famous after getting into the adult biz in 2021.

title: Cheerleader Mom Murder-Suicide: 11-Year-Old Addi Was Full of Drugs When Killed
description:
Cheerleader Mom Murder-Suicide
                          11-Year-Old Had Body Full of Drugs
body:
Cheerleader Mom Murder-Suicide
                          11-Year-Old Had Body Full of Drugs
                          ... Suicide Notes Found
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 15, 2026
                            11:30 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 15, 2026
                                12:13 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The girl who authorities say was killed by her mother in a hotel room at a cheerleading competition had numerous drugs in her system before the apparent murder-suicide ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            TMZ obtained the Clark County Medical Examiner report for 11-year-old Addi Smith, who was allegedly killed by her mom, Tawnia McGeehan, inside their Vegas hotel room in February 2026 ... and it says Addi had a smorgasbord of substances in her system.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The medical report said Addi was found in her pajamas with a pillow covering her face. Officers believed Addi was "very medicated" before being shot by her mom. The report notes a suicide note was found at the scene.
      

            The coroner found several drugs in the girl's blood, including quetiapine (an antipsychotic used to treat depression, schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder), diphenhydramine (the active ingredient in Benadryl), and Lorazepam (a benzodiazepine used to treat anxiety and insomnia).
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The pair were in town for a cheer competition, but cops were called for a welfare check after Addi's dad had not heard from her in a while.
      
    
            As TMZ first reported, officers found a note outside the door warning them to call 911 due to "two dead bodies" being inside the room.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The report also noted weed gummies and a ton of prescription drug bottles in Tawnia's name around the room. A Ruger handgun was also found in the room.
      
    
            The official cause of death was listed as a gunshot wound to the head for both Tawnia and Addi.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Tawnia also had several drugs in her system when she died.
